articles.title: Omar raid outrage goes from bad to worse when internet notices her past 6-word claim: 'Couldn't agree more'
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided by DHS agents in a fraud investigation, and her old "no one is above the law" quote resurfaced fast.
articles.body: Reactions immediately started pouring in after federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., with many on social media pointing to a previous claim from Omar that "no one" is above the law. Omar’s home was raided by agents with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) investigation unit in the early Monday morning hours, Fox News Digital first reported, in a search that stems from a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child. Omar has been under fire for months and faced a myriad of controversies during her time in Congress, most recently, her financial disclosures have come into focus, and questions have been raised by top officials about her path to citizenship as well. Many on social media were quick to point to a previous comment from Omar where she declared that "no one is above the law" after Trump was indicted in a hush money case that conservatives argued was based on flimsy evidence and a political prosecution. OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP' "Rather than issue our own statement, we'll defer to Rep. Omar," the Minnesota Republican Party posted on X. "She said it best back in 2023, when the subject of a criminal investigation was someone else." "We couldn't agree more, Congresswoman. We're sure you still feel the same way now that it's your front door. Minnesotans will be watching closely, and so will we." "No one is above the law," the Trump War Room account posted on X. "It was an authorized search warrant approved by a federal judge as part of a criminal investigation," conservative influencer LibsofTikTok posted on X. "No one is above the law." "Ilhan Omar was right," Townhall columnist Dustin Grage posted on X. "Nobody is above the law." "No one is above the law," Charlie Kirk Show executive producer Andrew Kolvet posted on X. "(And etting [sic] lectured by a Somali about the rule of law is rich. Not as rich as Rep. Omar was before she revised her financial statements, but rich.)" "So much for ‘no one is above the law,’" conservative commentator Viva Frei posted on X. CAUGHT ON CAMERA: SQUAD DEM SQUIRMS WHEN PRESSED ON VANCE DOJ FRAUD PROBE Omar released a response to the raid accusing the Trump administration of improperly targeting her. "I’m ok," Omar wrote on X hours after the search commenced. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Fox News Digital reached out to Omar’s office for comment. "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investgations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital. The DOJ later added that the investigation was "criminal" in nature.

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: As the House falls, the Senate stays in play
articles.summary: Democrats' generic ballot lead is wider than the 2018 blue wave, pushing the House forecast toward a potential 237-seat Democratic majority.
articles.body: There are two big differences between the previous Trump-era midterms and this year’s contest. The first is the president’s approval rating, which is lower now than it was during President Donald Trump’s first term in 2018 or President Joe Biden’s term in 2022. The second is Democrats’ generic ballot lead, which is wider and more enduring than it was in the 2018 "blue wave" election and much larger than the edge the GOP had in 2022. Combined with Democrats’ candidate quality improvements and a Republican-led redistricting effort that could fall short of expectations, the House is likely out of reach for the GOP this year. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. Then there’s a similarity: in all three elections, the Senate has been in play right up until the finish line. In Trump’s first term, the Republicans ended up gaining two Senate seats despite a gloomy national environment. Four years ago, with inflation surging, the Democrats managed to add a Senate seat to their tally. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK The Democrats have plentiful paths to 51 seats on election night. Republicans keep plowing money into six toss-up states, plus Kansas, and those efforts haven’t much moved the needle. Yet the GOP’s paths to 50 are getting wider. That, plus a major update to the House forecast, in this week’s edition of the Power Rankings. House: Democrats set to take control with up to 237 seats The Democratic Party has enjoyed a lead in the House all year. Now, as another 20 races shift leftward, this forecast sees the Democrats taking control. THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER Democrats have an advantage in at least 219 seats, while Republicans should hold on to at least 198 seats. There are 18 toss-ups on the board. On a good night for the Democrats, the party will hold around 237 seats, or a gain of 22 from their current position. That’s because toss-up seats have mostly fallen in one party’s direction in previous elections. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG? (A "great night" for the Democrats, which would see the party take some Lean R seats as well, would mean a Democratic majority of up to 249.) If the toss-up seats go the other way, the GOP could make life hard for the left. A good night for Republicans would see the party end up with around 216 seats. That’s two short of a majority but also leaves the Democrats with a mere two-vote cushion in the House. In that scenario, a coalition of far-left Democrats, like the "Squad" of years past, could band together to put policy pressure on the next House speaker. That group is about to get bigger, thanks to the sure-thing victories of Democratic Socialists like Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez. Some of this week’s shifts are a product of polling. The Democrats’ generic ballot lead has pushed districts like Kentucky’s 6th District (Lexington and its suburbs) and Texas’ 15th District (Rio Grande Valley and Coastal Bend) away from the GOP. The party’s strength in statewide races also plays a role, especially in Iowa (the 1st and 3rd districts, which contain the state’s biggest cities), and in Pennsylvania (three districts have shifted to the left, thanks in part to Governor Josh Shapiro’s coattails). Other shifts are the result of Republican groups moving resources elsewhere, like from New York’s 19th District. Democratic Rep. Josh Riley lost this race by fewer than 5,000 votes four years ago, but as the GOP sends its money to more winnable races, it’s moving to Solid D. A more surprising theme is also emerging: the GOP is in trouble with rural voters. Sitting above Albany, New York’s 21st District contains some of the state’s most rural areas. Its voters delivered President Trump a 21-point victory over Vice President Harris two years ago. A survey last week had the Democratic candidate four points ahead of the Republican, 46%-42%. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS Maine’s 2nd District, which famously voted for President Trump three times in a row – and last time by nine points – is an open race this year after Rep. Jared Golden’s retirement. It was thought to be one of the best flip opportunities for the GOP. A new poll has the Democrat at 51% and the Republican at 45%. Even Virginia’s 5th District, stretching across the Southside region and home to a two-thirds rural population, is a six-point race in a recent survey (45%-51% with the Republican ahead). The Democrat, Tom Perriello, was recently endorsed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Gas, diesel and grocery prices are to blame. In dollar terms, the cost of living is higher in cities and suburbs, but voters across the country keep saying they are feeling the pressure of those increases and blame Republicans for them. Iowa, for example, has experienced the fourth-highest gas price hike in the nation. Kentucky, Ohio and Texas are all in the top five states for diesel increases. That has proven tough for GOP candidates to counter. New York’s 21st District moves from Solid R to Likely R. (Virginia’s 5th and Maine’s 2nd districts remain at Lean R and Toss-up, respectively.) Senate: Michele Tafoya plays offense in Minnesota The Senate is still a toss-up with Democrats and Republicans taking 47 seats apiece. Six toss-ups are the most likely to determine control. If Democrats win all six of those states, the party will take the majority with two seats to spare, for a total of 53. On the other hand, this forecast still sees a pathway for the GOP not to lose any seats. They’d accomplish that just by holding on to the same six states. The toss-ups have largely been locked in through summer. There’s been a lot more movement in the "lean" categories (Kansas in, Georgia and North Carolina out). Collectively, you can think of these as the election night battlegrounds. This week, a ninth state joins the list: Minnesota. The North Star State has been on the political radar since Republicans recruited Michele Tafoya, the former NFL sideline reporter. She has deftly navigated her foray into politics by focusing on fraud, crime, and the cultural issues that animate GOP voters. She also has a favorable matchup against Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s sitting lieutenant governor. It’s not clear whether Flanagan’s progressive politics or her proximity to the fraud issue is giving voters pause. Whatever the cause, there are signs that they are. A new gold-standard survey shows 47% of likely voters support Flanagan, while 43% back Tafoya. Another 9% are undecided. Republicans are fully united behind Tafoya, while 9-in-10 Democrats say they’ll support Flanagan’s bid. Independents are much less settled: 38% back Tafoya, 32% support Flanagan, and 29% haven’t decided. Minnesota’s voter profile and election history suggest that there are some left-of-center voters in the "independent" column. They may be wavering on Flanagan now, then show up to vote for her on election day. The Senate hopeful’s spot on the ballot next to Amy Klobuchar, the Democrats’ gubernatorial candidate and electoral over-performer, may also help push her over the line. articles.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog lawsuit seeking records on Elon Musk’s DOGE
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear arguments in a watchdog’s lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk’s Department...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear arguments in a watchdog's lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency.

The high court is intervening for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington's case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term. The Trump administration asked the court to hear the case.

Last year, the high court reined in a district court's order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court's conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group.

CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act.

The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA's requirements as a presidential advisory body.

Cooper ruled in CREW's favor and ordered expedited processing of the group's records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW.

The Trump administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court's direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the "autonomy and confidentiality" of presidential advisers.

"Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA's reach," Justice Department attorneys wrote .

The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorized the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason.

CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court's previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025.

"Undisputed facts in the public record — including the President's statements — confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government," its attorneys wrote .

In a statement Tuesday, CREW attorney Nikhel Sus said the lower courts have uniformly ruled that it is entitled to records that could help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to the Freedom of Information Act.

"We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration's efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government," Sus said in the statement.

articles.title: Trump-linked super PAC pulls funding from 2 House Republicans as GOP fights to keep majority
articles.summary: House Republicans face growing pressure as Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. pulls planned spending from Tom Kean and Marianette Miller-Meeks' districts.
articles.body: A top elections group affiliated with President Donald Trump is halting spending planned in two key congressional districts held by sitting House Republicans as Election Day looms less than a month away. MAGA Inc. is reallocating its planned investments in districts represented by Rep. Tom Kean, R-N.J., and Rep. Marianette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, for the remainder of the midterm election cycle, a source familiar with those plans confirmed to Fox News Digital. A super PAC aligned with House GOP leadership, the Congressional Leadership Fund (CLF), is also pulling its cash from those districts to reroute into other races, a source familiar with those plans said. Both groups will instead route those funds into other House races across the country. It comes after recent polling data signaled the two incumbents' chances for re-election have grown slim. WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN Republicans' uphill battle to keep control of the House of Representatives is getting tougher by the day, according to various projections. The latest Fox News Power Rankings show Democrats having an edge in 219 House seats — enough to clinch a majority — while Republicans are projected to keep 198. Nineteen seats are still up in the air. Kean's 7th Congressional District is one of the wealthiest in both New Jersey and the U.S. as a whole, encompassing suburbs and exurbs of New York City to the north. A source close to Kean's campaign told Fox News Digital that "the race is fully funded down the home stretch." Kean's campaign and House Republicans' campaign arm "have major reservations on broadcast," the source said, adding that his Democratic opponent Rebecca Bennett "has no soft dollar reservations on her behalf." He and Miller-Meeks represent two of the most purple districts in the country. Kean won his House seat in 2022 after defeating incumbent former Rep. Tom Malinowski, D-N.J., by less than 10,000 votes. His 2024 re-election margin was wider, winning by just over 5%, or 23,000 more votes than his Democrat challenger. Miller-Meeks, meanwhile, is seeking a fourth term against Democrat Christina Bohannan, whom she defeated twice by roughly 20,000 and 800 votes in 2022 and 2024. She first won in 2020 by just six votes — earning her the nickname "six-pack" among fellow House Republicans and GOP leadership. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS Miller-Meeks represents Iowa's 1st Congressional District in the state's southeast, encompassing the cities of Davenport and Iowa City. The New York Times first reported plans by "top Republican super PACs aligned with President Trump and congressional Republican leadership" to pull funding from Kean and Miller-Meeks' districts over concerns about their polling. TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO CLF is reportedly pulling the funding as part of a wider reshuffling of its war chest into other districts that Republicans are more confident in. That includes battleground Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., and Monica De La Cruz, R-Texas, The Times reported. The source familiar with CLF's planning told Fox News Digital the group was also pulling funding from Michigan's 8th Congressional District and Ohio's 1st Congressional District, where Republicans were hoping to unseat Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., and Greg Landsman, D-Ohio. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Miller-Meeks' campaign but did not immediately hear back.

articles.title: It’s time to deliver safe and effective psychedelic medicine
articles.summary: Congressional leaders Jack Bergman and Lou Correa called for the establishment of national standards and a regulatory framework to safely integrate psychedelic-assisted therapies into the U.S. healthcare system.
articles.body:
America faces a mental health crisis, and sadly, our federal government is not keeping pace. Every day, over 130 Americans die by suicide, including over 20 veterans per day. Psychedelic-assisted therapies have emerged as a promising new alternative for treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic-stress disorder, substance use disorders, and generalized anxiety disorder.

But instead of receiving these therapies here in the U.S., our veterans and other Americans are going abroad in search of these often lifesaving psychedelic-assisted therapies.

We are grateful for the Trump administration’s work to accelerate research on these therapies and the Food and Drug Administration’s granting of Breakthrough Therapy designation to multiple psychedelic-based drug products, including psilocybin and MDMA. But more needs to be done at the federal level to ensure safe and effective therapies reach the people who need them the most.

Two years ago, our bipartisan Congressional Psychedelics Advancing Therapies or “PATH” Caucus issued a formal request for information , asking for feedback on how we can safely and effectively integrate psychedelic medicine into the U.S. health care system.

Respondents made clear that psychedelics are not necessarily magic bullets. But if delivered in a safe and structured environment, they can be transformative for American patients. And that is exactly why we need new federal policies that create nationwide standards for the safe use of these treatments in medical settings. We need a national framework to ensure safe and equitable access.

Responses to our PATH Caucus request for information point toward a pragmatic path of accelerating legitimate medical development while building strong guardrails for safety, ethics and equity. That begins with national standards for service delivery and practitioner credentialing.

Stakeholders across the spectrum agree that our nation needs guidance and verification systems in place before the coming FDA approvals of psychedelic therapies. We also need labeling requirements for psychedelic medicine and the codification of best practices for “set and setting,” crisis response, and pre- and post-session integration support.

If we want to fulfill the full public health potential of psychedelic medicine, Congress and federal agencies also need to tackle these issues head-on. It’s no longer a matter of if psychedelic-assisted therapies will enter the American health care system, but when.

All attention must focus on how we can integrate them safely and effectively, so that patients in need can access these treatments. We must seize this moment by establishing a coherent set of standards that protect patients, deliver equitable access, and yield life-enhancing benefits for every American suffering from severe mental and physical health challenges.

Jack Bergman represents Michigan’s 1st Congressional District and is a retired Marine Corps lieutenant general. Lou Correa represents California’s 46th Congressional District. Both members serve as co-chairs of the Congressional PATH Caucus.

articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is heading to Florida over the weekend to campaign for Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate.

Sanders has crisscrossed the country in recent months to turn out support for Democratic Senate candidates, including Troy Jackson in Maine, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

The Vermont senator will join Nixon, a state lawmaker, at four events around the state on Saturday and Sunday in Tampa, Gainesville, Tallahassee and Melbourne. Nixon, a democratic socialist, has been criticized by some more mainstream Democrats since winning her August primary. She faces an uphill battle in the red state against incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida).

Sanders and Nixon share a progressive identity. Nixon is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America while Sanders, although not a member, has long identified with the movement. She also supports “Medicare for All,” Sanders’s hallmark universal health care plan, free childcare, a national rent freeze and “taxing billionaires,” among other policies that mirror Sanders’s platform.

Sanders endorsed Nixon in August and, earlier this month, donated $250,000 to the Florida Democratic Party to support her and other Democrats in the state.

“Angie’s campaign is proof that Democratic voters are looking for candidates who will fight for them and who will take on the greed of the billionaire class,” Sanders said in a statement when he endorsed Nixon.

articles.body:
President Trump is set to host a Kentucky rally this weekend as part of his midterm blitz . The event is in support of Trump-endorsed GOP candidate Ed Gallrein, who is running for Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-K.Y.) congressional seat.

The rally is scheduled for Saturday in Highland Heights, a town in Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District that has voted red for the House since 2002, according to the Republican National Committee. Massie lost in the GOP primary to Gallrein, who faces Democrat Melissa Strange next month.

Massie became an adversary of Trump’s over the release of the Epstein files and the Iran war . He said in September, the president’s “comeuppance will happen on Election Day.”

The rally’s site, near the border of Ohio, falls within Cincinnati’s media market. It marks the third visit by Trump to the region as the GOP seeks to defend vulnerable candidates.

Though Trump carried Ohio in each of his presidential bids — winning it by more than 11 percentage points in 2024 — the red-leaning Buckeye State governor’s mansion has the potential to flip.

Democrat Amy Acton leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 8 percentage points, according to a new CNN poll . Decision Desk HQ’s, a partner of The Hill, polling averages now show Acton up roughly 4 points, rating the race a toss-up.

Trump and his allies hope this campaign blitz in red and purple districts will help to energize base voters. His stops in Ohio so far have included rallies in Dayton and Youngstown. Vice President Vance traveled last week to Lima for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

Husted — who was appointed to fill Vance’s old Senate seat — is seeking his first full term against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) in a year where the GOP is on the defensive amid growing voter dissatisfaction over rising gas and grocery prices , partially because of the ongoing war in Iran.

A Suffolk University poll released late last month showed the former senator leading Husted 47 percent to 44 percent among registered voters, while a CNN/SSRS poll released in October showed Brown leading 49 percent to 43 percent among registered voters.

articles.title: Americans draw the line at livestreaming ‘spectacle’ of Fort Hood shooter's execution: ‘It’s an abomination’
articles.summary: Americans blast Pete Hegseth's plan to livestream convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution as "absolutely absurd" and dangerous.
articles.body: Americans are overwhelmingly against the Pentagon's decision to livestream the firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan later this year. Those who spoke with Fox News Digital blasted the broadcast as "a shame" and "just weird." "I think that's absolutely absurd," Anya from Virginia said when asked about the livestream announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. "I think they should keep that discreet and off of the public news." "It's an abomination. It should not happen," Paul from Illinois definitively stated. "And I'd hate to be one of the soldiers that's tasked with the job of pulling the trigger." Hegseth announced last Thursday the decision to make viewing the execution publicly available. It is set to be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades. PENTAGON CONFIRMS FORT HOOD TERRORIST'S FIRING SQUAD EXECUTION WILL BE LIVESTREAMED: 'DETAILS WILL FOLLOW' The execution of the mass shooter who killed 13 people and injured 32 in 2009 at Fort Hood, is scheduled for Dec. 3, 2026. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shooting, is now 56 years old and is wheelchair-bound after he was left partially paralyzed after being shot by police officers during his arrest almost 17 years ago. Several Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital supported Hasan's death sentence but drew the line at broadcasting his execution, warning it could turn capital punishment into a public spectacle and could be particularly dangerous in today's political climate. "I'm not necessarily against giving him the death penalty, but I feel like livestreaming for people's entertainment is just weird," Nick from Virginia said. "I agree with the sentence," Bobbie from Massachusetts said. "I don't agree with televising it." He added, "Especially given the climate of today, I'm not sure it's something we need to see." "It’s not a practice we should be doing in modern society," Reid from Ohio said. "It's rather medieval, in my opinion. I'm certainly pro-death penalty for heinous crimes such as that, but I think that … turns it into something of a spectacle that it really doesn't have any business being." FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD But one Virginia man took a drastically different position, suggesting the government should charge Americans to watch the execution and donate the proceeds to the family of U.S. service members who died in the line of duty. "I think they're missing an opportunity," Jason from Virginia said. "It should be pay-per-view and all the proceeds should go to Gold Star families." He continued, "You have someone who was a murderous traitor to our country. And there's not a lot of coverage about that. So I think the public needs and deserves to know the consequences to, well, FAFO." Some raised concerns that the execution leaves children vulnerable to possibly accessing or being exposed to watching Hasan die on livestream. "We have enough violence in our society," William from Virginia said. "I'm pretty sure he's guilty, but it doesn't need to be public. Children could be watching that." "I just don't think that stuff like that should be put on the mainstream," Ferris from Massachusetts said. "Especially considering that children may have access to seeing it." Another pointed out Hasan’s health status, arguing the issue could be approached differently if he was "up and around" but citing the shooter’s well-being as a reason he sees the livestreamed execution as that much more wrong. "You're executing somebody who's not mentally stable, who is in this wheelchair situation," one respondent told Fox News Digital. The Trump administration’s announcement of the livestream was largely widely seen as a power play for the United States, demonstrating the consequences of committing such an act of terror on American soil — particularly committing violence toward members of the U.S. military. "I think they're trying to make an example out of him, you know?" Nick said. "I think it's like a show of power. They're trying to be like … 'Don't mess with us.'" GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT "I think it's a message that we're big and tough, and we don't have much humanity left," Paul said. Trump said Saturday that he will make the decision of whether to livestream Hasan’s execution, acknowledging that he knows "what the military would like to do" following Hegseth’s confirmation. "The world's gone crazy," Anya said. "We need Jesus."

articles.body:
It’s Tuesday. The news never sleeps, and that is why we thrive on coffee. ☕

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Steff Danielle Thomas , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

The scandal surrounding Kimberly Guilfoyle , U.S. ambassador to Greece, came to a head on Tuesday morning after White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said in her first press briefing that the administration has asked Guilfoyle to resign.

It was first reported by The Wall Street Journal last week that Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters to a pay $100,000 credit card bill.

Hiding the evidence: Not only did Guilfoyle apparently ask Deters for a little cash but she requested he do the transaction through a wire transfer to not leave a paper trail, The Hill’s Julia Manchester wrote.

The Wall Street Journal also reported over the weekend that Deters allegedly helped fund Guilfoyle’s luxury vacations to promote their business interests.

Following the Deters report, the accusations mounted against Guilfoyle, who was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and engaged to Donald Trump Jr.

Guilfoyle responds : The former ambassador responded to the resignation on the social platform X, saying that the “allegations are false.”

“I will forever be grateful to President Donald J. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the world,” Guilfoyle wrote.

“I also want to address the recent allegations against me,” she continued. “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

“Detering” in the wrong direction: Deters said in an interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Monday that he would be suing Guilfoyle over false claims allegedly made by her legal team.

“I’m going to be suing those lawyers, that law firm and Kimberly Guilfoyle,” Deters said. “It’s going to be fun.”

“They first said that the text messages were fake — defamation. Then they said I was a known blackmailer. I’ve never blackmailed anybody in my life,” Deters continued.

Deters told the Journal that he paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over the last several years to speak at a Kentucky-based event called Freedom Fest.

Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek (D) and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) are neck-and-neck in polling for retiring Sen. Joni Ernest’s (R-Iowa) seat, with their second debate scheduled for Tuesday night.

First debate fireworks: During the first debate, the pair discussed the Iran war and its impact on rising fuel prices — something Hinson has split on with President Trump in recent weeks.

“I don’t want this to be a forever war, so I want to make sure we do everything we can,” Hinson said.

Turek has called out Hinson for her early support in the Iran war and Trump’s tariffs, saying that diesel prices are at an “all-time high” for the state’s farmers thanks to the conflict.

Occasional agreements: The Democratic candidate broke with his party on multiple occasions during the debate, including his emphasis on protecting the southern border.

Hinson has backed Trump’s immigration enforcement, but Turek jabbed Hinson on not backing immigration violations in 2024.

“I’m the only one up on this stage that has actually worked across the aisle to address immigration,” Turek said.

Turek also noted that he had no interest in impeaching the president, and that “we need to look forward, not back.”

Hinson has had her own splits from the GOP on maternal healthcare and veterans’ mental health bills that were signed under former President Biden.

What do polls show?: A survey released by Emerson College last week had Hinson leading Turek by 2 points, with 47 percent and 45 percent support respectively.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, stated that Hinson is “narrowly favored” over Turek, and The Cook Political Report has rated the race a “toss-up.”

President Trump will headline a midterm rally in Wasilla, Alaska, Tuesday night amid the highly contested Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D).

The president’s visit comes a week after Vice President Vance held a midterm rally in Fairbanks to help push Sullivan ahead near the finish line.

Last week, the president slammed Alaska’s new nonpartisan voting system, where residents will have the chance to vote for one of four Senate and governor candidates.

“We have the Corrupt Ranked Choice System of Voting, which shouldn’t be allowed in our Country and will, hopefully, be repealed in the November Vote,” Trump wrote last week on Truth Social.

Peltola vs. Sullivan tightens: According to DDHQ, Peltola leads Sullivan by 3.4 percentage points as of Tuesday.

Trump has endorsed Sullivan in the Senate race and Republican Nick Begich in the House race.

Trump’s surprise diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin is creating a political headache for Republicans just three weeks before the midterms — and it’s not clear whether it will actually bring down prices.

articles.summary: Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) applauded President Trump’s “willingness to act” on the financial fraud allegations against former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle — who resigned Tuesday morning. “I commend the Administration for taking the allegations involving Ambassador Guilfoyle seriously,” the senator wrote on social platform X. “Public service is a public trust, and political…
articles.body:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) applauded President Trump’s “willingness to act” on the financial fraud allegations against former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle — who resigned Tuesday morning.

“I commend the Administration for taking the allegations involving Ambassador Guilfoyle seriously,” the senator wrote on social platform X . “Public service is a public trust, and political connections should never put anyone above accountability.”

“I appreciate President Trump’s willingness to act. That’s the kind of leadership Americans are yearning for,” he concluded.

Guilfoyle’s resignation was announced Tuesday morning by new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia following backlash over her financial dealings. Guilfoyle later released a resignation statement on the social platform X.

The Wall Street Journal first reported last week that Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 credit card bill and instructed him to do so via wire transfer to avoid a paper trail.

The outlet also reported new allegations that wealthy Greek businessmen helped fund Guilfoyle’s luxury travel as she used her role to promote their business interests.

In her resignation statement, Guilfoyle denied these allegations, calling them “false ,” and stated her intention “to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

“I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,” she wrote.

After the announcement, Trump said the influx of negative press stories surrounding Guilfoyle led to the ousting.

“She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump said to reporters outside of the White House.

Curtis has been critical of some recent moves by the Trump administration — including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would be livestreamed.

In a statement shared to social media, Curtis recalled Seneca warning Rome that “bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them,” adding that “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”

“Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite,” he continued. “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”

articles.title: GOP senators condemn Trump’s Russia diesel deal as ‘betrayal of our allies’
articles.summary: A growing group of Republican senators is condemning President Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import an estimated 2.5 million tons of Russian diesel as a “gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies.” Six Republican senators, including former Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (Ky.) and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), signed a…
articles.body:
A growing group of Republican senators is condemning President Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import an estimated 2.5 million tons of Russian diesel as a “gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies.”

Six Republican senators, including former Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (Ky.) and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), signed a bipartisan letter to Trump Tuesday slamming the president’s agreement to buy hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, despite a 2022 law prohibiting such a purchase without notification to Congress, as a grave mistake.

“The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans,” they wrote, warning that lifting sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports “only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians.”

Republican Sens. Alan Armstrong (Okla.), Thom Tillis (N.C.), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), and Susan Collins (Maine) also signed the letter. Tillis was the lead Republican signatory.

Six Democrats also signed it: Sen. Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), the lead Democratic signatory, and Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), Dick Durbin (Ill.), Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Jack Reed (R.I.) and Chris Coons (Del.).

The senators acknowledged that Trump is trying to lower high diesel prices , which reached a record high of $6.53 a gallon last month, but they warned the import of Russian diesel would have little impact on prices in the United States.

“Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans. It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance security cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea,” they wrote.

They warned that could ultimately “endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury,” referring to the military conflict with Iran.

The senators circulated the letter a day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia violated a ceasefire by striking at least six energy targets across Ukraine.

Zelensky warned that allowing Russia to collect more revenue from energy sales would fund “its war machine.”

The GOP senators and their Democratic colleagues noted that last month Congress passed and Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which granted Trump authorities to apply economic pressure on Russia and its economic partners, such as China, to enhance the U.S. negotiating position to bring an end to the four-year-old Ukraine war.

“For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation’s resistance to tyrants. Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Rian Act,” the wrote, referring to the Treasury Department’s general license lifting Russia sanctions.

“Maintain our legacy — and the duty America holds — as leader of the free world,” the wrote.

Tuesday’s letter followed a joint statement a bipartisan group of senators, including Collins, Murkowski, Tillis and Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) released on Sunday pointing out that Congress “explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.”

Curtis did not sign the Tuesday letter to Trump.

articles.title: Ziwe destroys Hasan Piker in amazing interview: bravo!
articles.summary: Ziwe, my hat’s off to you.
articles.body:
Ziwe is a comedian and YouTuber who does funny interviews with notable people in which she knocks them down a peg by pointing out their hypocrisies and inconsistencies. And she did this extremely well with her latest guest, Hasan Piker . In fact, she did a better job than many people in the mainstream media, who have asked Piker about his controversial statements but not really gotten to the bottom of why he is a ridiculous attention-seeking fool and also a loathsome political extremist.

Indeed, what Ziwe did so successfully is point out the absurdity of Piker looking and acting and even dressing like a communist, while he lives richly and is in fact a privileged nepo baby who got his start in media career because of his uncle, Cenk Uygur.

And while I’ve pointed this out before, I feel compelled to do so again: Wearing the suit of Chairman Mao, a brutal dictator whose economic policies caused widespread famine that killed millions, is really not super different, in my opinion, from wearing a Nazi suit. People would not think fondly of somebody who did the latter, and so we should not give Piker a pass for doing the former.

Unfortunately, while we all accept that fascists were evil, brutal killers, sometimes the media fails to call attention to the significant number of atrocities committed by communists. Piker is either unaware of communist evils or doesn’t care, or even supports them.

In a detailed takedown of Piker, The Atlantic’s Jonathan Chait delves deeply into the supportive things he has said about communist regimes over the years.

Piker has even praised North Korea! He said, “it’s certainly not as bad as the way that Western media presents it,” and that the country’s meager economic progress over the years “shows you that a better future is possible for all of us.” He thinks the U.S. should aspire to have North Korean levels of success. This would of course necessitate going massively backward as a nation and as a people, and enshrining an appalling autocracy. Because, make no mistake, North Korea is one of the most oppressive places on earth.

Chait writes in summary that Piker is correct to complain he is often quoted out of context — but that’s because the context makes his quotes much worse.

But back to the Ziwe interview. She calls out Piker for mocking a Vietnamese refugee who had been warning about the dangers of communism. Here is how Piker answered that accusation : He said, yeah, I mocked her, and I was right do so.

I think that really gets to the heart of why he is such an utterly repellant figure. Piker has contempt for everyone who is not as far left as he is, and that includes pretty much everybody. And he’s just utterly indifferent to the actual existing suffering under communist regimes, historically and at present, which was and is several orders of magnitude worse than anything the Trump administration has done.

Now, maybe you think I’m wasting my time spending so much oxygen on a Twitch streamer. Certainly conservative media has gone overboard in airing their grievances with him. What I’m worried about is not so much Piker himself, but what he represents and where independent left media is headed.

Is this the future? Someone who cosplays as Mao and thinks it’s cool to shout down anti-communist dissidents? Who blasts the billionaires from the comforts of first class or his million-dollar mansion or the Oscars after parties? Who wants to take over the Democratic Party and staff it with people who admire foreign extremists and passionately hate moderation, decency, and essentially all the things that make American great?

So again, kudos to Ziwe for making Piker look ridiculous, because he is ridiculous.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Why these roller coasters are closed after a rider’s death at Six Flags in Georgia
articles.summary: Nine other Six Flags attractions have been closed.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – An investigation is underway and several roller coasters across the U.S. have been shuttered after a man fell to his death at a Six Flags near Atlanta on Monday.

The man, identified as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta, appeared to have been “ejected” from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, the Cobb County Police Department said Tuesday. He “struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction,” where he was found “unresponsive and not breathing.”

Logan Conner, who was on Goliath at the same time, told NBC that Kariem was “levitating in the air sideways.”

“We made direct eye contact with him,” he recounted.

Authorities said they were still investigating what caused the incident. They did not give an update on those who were injured on the ride.

Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, meanwhile, has since temporarily closed nine other roller coasters across six of its parks. A park spokesperson told Nexstar’s NewsNation that the closures are “out of an abundance of caution.”

Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Illinois

Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain near Los Angeles

Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey

Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in North Carolina

Orion and Diamondback at Kings Island near Cincinnati

Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada’s Wonderland

These parks were already scheduled for seasonal midweek closures on Tuesday and Wednesday.

While the spokesperson didn’t expand on why these rides were shuttered, all but one were manufactured by the Swiss-based Bolliger & Mabillard. Goliath at Magic Mountain was manufactured by Giovanola. Bolliger & Mabillard did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Nexstar, but said in a statement obtained by The Associated Press that it was “actively investigating the incident [in Georgia] and will not comment further until we have a better understanding of what happened.”

“We are deeply saddened by this tragic accident,” the company said in a statement. “Our thoughts are with the family and those affected.”

Goliath is described as a “hypercoaster,” as are Nitro and Diamondback. According to Bolliger & Mabillard, hypercoasters are “focused on speed, airtime, and towering views.” They feature the company’s “innovative lap bar restraint design [which] provides an incomparable feeling of freedom.”

Georgia’s Goliath is the slowest and shortest of the now-shuttered coasters, reaching speeds of 70 mph across 4,480 feet with an elevation of 200 feet. It falls behind Raging Bull in speed (73 mph) and elevation (202 feet), and California’s Goliath in distance (4,500 feet).

Both Goliath rides are considered fours on the five-point “Thrill Level” scale used by Six Flags. Six others – Diamondback, Orion, Thunder Striker, Fury 325, Nitro, and Raging Bull – are rated as fives.

In 2006, when Georgia’s Goliath opened, a man died after likely having a heart attack on the coaster, said Doan Law Firm, which tallies amusement park accidents and represents victims. Kariem is at least the seventh person to die at the Georgia park since 1989.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump on Russia, Ukraine attacks: ‘They’re both a little off’
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday appeared to defend Russia’s continued strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure a day after he announced an “energy ceasefire” that he claimed Moscow had agreed to. “Ukraine hit many sites the day before,” Trump told reporters when asked about Russia’s continued missile and drone attacks on Monday. “They’re both a little bit…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday appeared to defend Russia’s continued strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure a day after he announced an “energy ceasefire” that he claimed Moscow had agreed to.

“Ukraine hit many sites the day before,” Trump told reporters when asked about Russia’s continued missile and drone attacks on Monday. “They’re both a little bit off.”

Speaking to journalists as he departed the White House on Tuesday, Trump insisted Ukraine and Russia wanted to end Moscow’s now five-year war against Kyiv, and that the U.S. is working with both sides to get to a resolution.

When asked if Russia had broken the ceasefire, Trump replied: “I’ll let you know about that later.”

“They’re hitting each other, but it’ll all come to an end. They both want it to come to an end, they just don’t know how to get there,” he added.

Trump stunned Ukraine, European allies and even Republican senators on Friday when he announced a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Moscow to export diesel to the United States — an effort to offset high fuel and diesel costs that have been driven up by the war in Iran.

But the agreement, which lifts sanctions on Russian diesel exports, is set to generate hundreds of millions of dollars for the Russian economy, putting it in a better position to continue its war against Ukraine. Under the plan, the U.S. would buy an estimated 2.5 million tons of fuel from the Kremlin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Trump “weak” for making the deal .

Angered by the response, Trump retaliated by having U.S. officials over the weekend call European capitals and Kyiv, threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons delivery through Europe if Ukraine refuses to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Trump was asked Tuesday whether the U.S. had cut off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and replied: “No we haven’t. We help them. But we’re really helping them get to a final answer, we want the war ended.”

He also appeared to distance himself from the diesel agreement with Russia, telling reporters it’s “a deal for the world,” and not with the U.S.

articles.title: Trump’s new press secretary raises eyebrows with bar exam response
articles.summary: President Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia raised eyebrows on Tuesday when she was asked where she passed the bar exam, telling reporters that she did so when she moved to China. Zacharia made the remarks on the White House South Lawn alongside Trump before heading to Alaska with him for a campaign rally. “Where…
articles.body:
President Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia raised eyebrows on Tuesday when she was asked where she passed the bar exam, telling reporters that she did so when she moved to China.

Zacharia made the remarks on the White House South Lawn alongside Trump before heading to Alaska with him for a campaign rally .

“Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?” a reporter asked Trump, who turned to Zacharia to ask her, “which state?”

“When I moved to China,” Zacharia responded.

When asked to confirm where Zacharia passed the bar exam, a White House official said she moved to China with her husband after graduating due to his job at a U.S private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law.

The newsletter Popular Information has previously raised questions around Zacharia’s legal career. It noted she has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer during appearances on Fox News on other outlets.

Pepperdine’s Caruso Law School congratulated Zacharia on the appointment, noting she was both an alumna and a member of its Dean’s Council.

However, it’s unclear if she ever passed the bar exam.

Asked for clarification Tuesday afternoon, she told NewsNation, “I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”

White House communications director Steven Cheung did not address questions about where Zacharia passed the bar exam in a response that praised her as a “fabulous and wonderful addition to the team.”

LinkedIn shows Katie has her JD from Pepperdine and worked as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing, China from Aug 2011-June 2013.

The South China Morning Post, and English-language newspaper in Hong Kong, highlighted Zacharia’s background in China for a story about her appointment , noting she worked for a non-profit organisation focused on the children.

Zacharia’s LinkedIn says she was “manager of fundraising and communications” for an organization called Compassion for Migrant Children. The Hill sent an email to an address listed on the website, which has not been updated for years.

In a biography included in her appointment to the advisory board of a mining company, Zacharia’s experience is said to include “legal, policy, and advisory matters across multiple jurisdictions and sectors.”

That includes “matters involving organizations associated with the World Bank Group and the International Finance Corporation during her tenure with Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing,” according to a press release from NovaRed Mining Inc, which has since changed its name.

The Hill reached out to Pepperdine and the American Bar Association on whether Zacharia has passed the bar.

Zacharia’s comments came after she conducted her first White House press briefing on Tuesday. The new press secretary took three questions during the briefing, which lasted just under fifteen minutes. She made news when she told a reporter that the administration had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece.

Trump announced he tapped Zacharia for the role on Friday.

While critics were quick to note Zacharia looked visibly nervous during the briefing, Trump and his allies praised her performance.

“I thought she was very good,” Trump told reporters before heading to Alaska on Tuesday.

Ava Thompson and Caroline Vakil contributed reporting.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton launching podcast ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton is launching a new podcast Wednesday focused on the final stretch of the midterm elections that will run through mid-November. Clinton will co-host “High Stakes” with tech journalist and former CNN host Kara Swisher, the former first lady posted on social media Tuesday. The Vox Media-produced series will be…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton is launching a new podcast Wednesday focused on the final stretch of the midterm elections that will run through mid-November.

Clinton will co-host “High Stakes” with tech journalist and former CNN host Kara Swisher, the former first lady posted on social media Tuesday. The Vox Media-produced series will be distributed through the same feed as Swisher’s “On” podcast.

“On Nov. 3, every seat in the House is on the ballot, along with 35 Senate seats and 36 governors,” Clinton said in a video. “What you pay for groceries, rent and healthcare is on the line. So I’m teaming up with Kara Swisher to dig into the issues that matter most before the country heads to the polls.”

The video ends with Swisher saying she approves this message, quipping that she “always wanted to say that.”

The podcast developed after Clinton and Swisher met at the home of former owner of The Atlantic David Bradley in Washington’s Kalorama neighborhood, The New York Times reported . After the two spoke and Swisher asked her questions on several topics, Swisher told the outlet that Clinton’s answers were “concise and intelligible,” leading to a test-run between the two on Swisher’s “Pivot” podcast.

“There’s a thing about the secretary, where it’s like, ‘Oh, if you knew her in the room, she’s so funny,'” Swisher told the Times. “We’re going to try to show you that room.”

Vox Media CEO Jim Bankoff told the newspaper that podcast equipment was sent to Clinton’s Chappaqua, N.Y., home.

Clinton noted that if the series draws a large enough audience, the podcast could continue further past the midterms, adding that she is willing to read her own ads.

“I don’t think the stakes for the country and the world could be any higher,” Clinton said about the podcast. “If we don’t reverse this chaos and corruption and cruelty that is being visited upon us by this administration, we won’t recognize our country.”

Clinton made her first endorsement in the midterms last week, backing Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) in her bid for the Senate. The former top diplomat used the endorsement to take a swipe at her 2016 presidential opponent, saying President Trump has made affordability a greater issue for voters.

“His tariffs and war in Iran are driving up prices, and his budget ripped healthcare and food assistance away from children so billionaires could get another tax cut,” Clinton said.

articles.title: Judge extends order blocking Trump administration from clearing trees at D.C. golf course
articles.summary: The judge presiding over a court fight over President Donald Trump’s plans for a public golf course in D.C. temporarily barred the removal of trees at the site.
articles.body: The judge presiding over a court fight involving President Donald Trump’s plans to redo a public golf course in Washington, D.C., issued an order Tuesday temporarily barring the administration from knocking down more trees at the site. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes handed down the order a day after an emergency hearing in which she accused the government of engaging in deception to knock down more than 400 trees at the East Potomac Golf Links over the holiday weekend. “The Court ORDERS that Defendants may not fell any further trees on the East Potomac Golf Course through Monday, October 26,” the judge wrote in a directive posted on the docket. Reyes is overseeing a lawsuit filed by a preservation group and two Washington residents challenging Trump’s golf course renovation. Earlier this year, she denied the plaintiffs’ request for a restraining order in the case after administration lawyers assured her they would give her and the plaintiffs ample notice of any large-scale work being done on the course. On Friday, attorneys for the Justice Department said in court papers filed shortly before 5 p.m. that the National Park Service would be removing roughly 500 trees from the course over the three-day holiday weekend. That work started Saturday morning, a park official testified in court Monday, and 430 trees were knocked down. The official, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess, said workers had identified about 300 more trees that still need to be cut down, but they weren’t able to work Sunday because of bad weather. Reyes told lawyers for the Justice Department at the hearing that she was “furious” with the government. “I was hearing from everyone on plaintiffs’ side this was going to happen. I said repeatedly, ‘No, I trust the government.’ I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” the judge said. “What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility,” Reyes added. The administration argued in a filing Friday that the work was for “maintenance activities” that were unrelated to Trump’s plans to transform the 100-year-old course into championship-style greens. It said it was implementing recommendations from a 2019 “Cultural Landscape Report” aimed at restoring the course closer to its original design. The plaintiffs, which include the D.C. Preservation League, scoffed at the argument in court papers, saying that there would have been no mad scramble to implement a years-old plan — and noting that Trump’s plan for the site would “require massive tree-clearing.” “Defendants would have this Court believe that this unprecedented operation is merely the sudden and purely coincidental fulfillment of recommendations posited in a Cultural Landscape Report seven years ago and is totally unrelated to the ongoing implementation of the Washington National plan,” they wrote. “Even if Defendants were entitled to the benefit of the doubt, they are not entitled to a suspension of disbelief,” they said. Reyes has demanded to know how the decision to chop down the trees came together. She initially ordered a follow-up hearing with testimony from a top official at the Interior Department on Tuesday but issued an order in the morning delaying the hearing until next Monday. She also directed National Park Service acting Director Jessica Bowron to appear. Reyes, a Biden-appointed judge, had made clear at a hearing last month that she’d been hoping to avoid issuing a restraining order in the case. “I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees. I am a judge,” she said then.

images.caption: A golfer pushes their bag cart past a stump on East Potomac Golf Course on Oct. 13, 2026 in Washington, D.C. A federal judge has ordered a halt on tree removal at East Potomac Golf Course after the Trump administration cut down at least 430 trees over the weekend.

articles.title: Most voters see Congress as out of touch on spending despite midterm affordability pitch
articles.summary: An overwhelming majority of voters believe current members of Congress are out of touch with their constituents’ monthly spending habits, even as both parties make affordability a central pitch to key voting blocs. An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll released Tuesday found that 86 percent of respondents believed their current congressmember or senator couldn’t…
articles.body:
An overwhelming majority of voters believe current members of Congress are out of touch with their constituents’ monthly spending habits, even as both parties make affordability a central pitch to key voting blocs.

An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll released Tuesday found that 86 percent of respondents believed their current congressmember or senator couldn’t accurately guess what they spend in a month, with 55 percent saying they thought lawmakers would guess too low while the other 31 percent expected lawmakers to guess too high.

Only 14 percent said they believed their lawmakers understood their monthly spending — underscoring the troubles Republicans face as the party in power as the Trump administration looks to quickly ameliorate inflation and cost of living issues before Election Day.

“When you ask [people] how they’re feeling about the economy, they don’t feel like things are getting better,” Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst, told The Hill.

“They feel like things are getting worse, and considering [President] Trump was elected … in large part, to address economic challenges, I think that is also not helping the GOP,” he noted.

The full results of the poll will be discussed Tuesday night on “Decision Desk 2026 Have Your Say: A NewsNation Town Hall” hosted by NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo.

Rahm Emanuel, former White House chief of staff; Stephen A. Smith, broadcaster and commentator; and Steve Bannon, former Trump strategist, will discuss what they see in the numbers during the Cuomo Town Hall.

Before voters elected him to the presidency for a second time, Trump vowed to lower prices after annual inflation spiked to a 40-year high in 2022.

But inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, increased from 3 percent in January 2025 to 3.4 percent in August of this year. The Iran war and the president’s ongoing tariff fight with Canada have put upward pressure on prices, as has the artificial intelligence build-out .

“The main thing you’re engaged with politically is the fact that my gas price is over $4 now at the gas pump, and … that’s going to breed frustration with the party in power, and the buck stops with the Republicans this time around,” Skelley told The Hill.

He added, “It’s about Trump in part, but it’s also about just certain political realities that the presidential party has always struggled to deal with, especially [when] people didn’t feel like things were going well.”

Despite persistent inflation , Americans are still spending. In September, credit and debit card spending per household was up 6.2 percent, according to the Bank of America Institute’s monthly survey.

Lower income households and the top 5 percent of households saw the fastest spending growth, at 5.5 percent and 5.9 percent, respectively.

But the survey found that spending outpaced wages last month, with lower-income wage growth falling from 4.7 percent in August to 4.5 percent in September.

Trump initially dismissed Americans’ concerns about affordability last year and has blasted Democratic lawmakers and candidates as “communists” on the campaign trail.

“If the Democrats win, you will have an economic depression the equivalent of 1929,” Trump said Monday at a rally in Ohio. “Our country’s going to go to hell. Your 401(k)s are going to be worthless.”

But the president has still appealed to voters’ pocketbooks ahead of the midterms, promising to send every American adult a $5,000 dividend if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

Trump reiterated that pledge Monday, telling rally attendees his administration can tap into money it has collected via tariffs to fund the dividends .

“If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country the likes of which we have never seen before,” the president said.

Trump’s pre-midterms economic agenda is not confined to promising $5,000 checks, either.

The Treasury Department has started sending $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans who, according to the department, were overcharged for their federal marketplace health insurance.

Roughly 20 million Medicare recipients will also receive an extra $90 this month from the Social Security Administration — money intended to assist enrollees pay for their Part B premiums.

On the food and energy fronts, Trump has recently announced an oil deal with Venezuela , reached an agreement for Russia to supply the American marketplace with diesel fuel and slashed tariffs on beef imports from Argentina and Brazil.

Yet, some Republicans are unsure that those moves will be enough to change the economic environment weeks out from the election.

“They have to be perceived by voters as being real and tangible, that these will likely happen,” explained GOP strategist Ron Bonjean.

“It doesn’t feel like it’s penetrated yet to that level,” he added.

The unfavorable economic environment bodes poorly for the GOP in the midterms, giving Democrats a chance to take control of both chambers of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s term.

The NewsNation/DDHQ survey found Democrats leading Republicans with 49 percent support to the GOP’s 42 percent on a generic congressional ballot. Democrats’ edge is just inside the question’s margin of error.

More than half of respondents also said they are voting to “oppose” Trump and his policies, while just a little more than a quarter said their support for the president is motivating them to cast a ballot.

And when the pollsters asked respondents what the country’s most urgent issues are, inflation ranked first at 28 percent, followed by jobs and the economy at 20 percent and immigration at 12 percent.

“Republicans have spent the last year and a half driving up prices while callously dismissing the economic pain Americans are feeling,” a spokesperson for Senate Democrats’ campaign arm said in a statement. “In November, voters will make sure that Republicans are the ones who pay the price at the ballot box.”

Still, while the recent polling points to bad signs for Republicans, Bonjean says the dissonance between voters and lawmakers ultimately hurts both parties.

“When an overwhelming majority of Americans believe their elected representatives do not understand what they spend every month, it’s a stunning disconnect,” Bonjean said.

“Until Washington closes that gap, economic trust is going to remain difficult to rebuild because it’s really earned … at the kitchen tables when families think that the politicians they’ve elected understand what they’re going through,” he added.

The NewsNation/DDHQ poll was conducted by AI research platform TrueDot.ai from Oct. 5-9, with 974 likely 2026 national voters surveyed. The margin of error for the full survey is 3.2 percentage points.

articles.title: Obama to campaign with Brown, Acton in Cleveland
articles.summary: Former President Obama is scheduled to hit the campaign trail with Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown (D) and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) at the end of the month. The former head of state will travel to Cleveland on Oct. 24 in an effort to boost support for the Democratic slate in the Buckeye State…
articles.body:
Former President Obama is scheduled to hit the campaign trail with Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown (D) and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) at the end of the month.

The former head of state will travel to Cleveland on Oct. 24 in an effort to boost support for the Democratic slate in the Buckeye State ahead of the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Both the Senate and gubernatorial races in Ohio are competitive this cycle, after years of the state trending red. Brown is trying to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R), who was appointed to the Senate by Gov. Mike DeWine (R) after JD Vance became Vice President, while Acton is up against biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy to be the state’s chief executive.

In an endorsement video released by Brown’s campaign on Tuesday, Obama praised the former U.S. senator for fighting for working people and encouraging job growth during his presidency.

“This race is going to be close,” the former president said. “It could determine which party controls the Senate and whether Ohioans can count on the people in Washington to be fighting for you.”

The fight for control of Congress is still tight with weeks to go until the election, with forecaster Decision Desk HQ predicting that Democrats have a 77 percent chance of winning back the House and a 56 percent chance of winning the Senate as of Tuesday.

President Trump traveled to Ohio on Monday to ramp up support for Husted and Ramaswamy as both candidates faced tight margins in recent polling. While the president encouraged his supporters to back the candidates in the November election, he also spent a considerable portion of his speech deriding Democrats like Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar (D).

Obama has taken on an active role in supporting Democratic campaigns across the country this election cycle.

The former commander-in-chief is scheduled to stump for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) and gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson (D) on the first day of in-person early voting in the state, which is also Oct. 24.

articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts 4 governors’ races toward Democrats
articles.summary: Cook Political Report is shifting four gubernatorial races in Democrats’ favor, the nonpartisan election handicapper said Tuesday, all in states which currently have Republican governors. Among the most notable shifts is Alaska, which moved from a “tossup” to “lean Democrat.” Three Republicans and one Democrat are vying for the state’s governor’s mansion, which is currently…
articles.body:
Cook Political Report is shifting four gubernatorial races in Democrats’ favor, the nonpartisan election handicapper said Tuesday, all in states which currently have Republican governors.

Among the most notable shifts is Alaska, which moved from a “tossup” to “lean Democrat.” Three Republicans and one Democrat are vying for the state’s governor’s mansion, which is currently held by GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy. In 2022, Dunleavy won reelection by more than 25 percentage points in a three-way race.

The rating shift in Alaska — as well as in Nebraska, Vermont and Oklahoma — come as polls show Democrats gaining ground in traditionally red areas less than a month out from November’s midterms.

Cook Political Report wrote that former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D-Alaska) is polling far ahead of the three Republican candidates in the race. Among the GOP’s nominees, conservative activist Bernadette Wilson is leading the pack.

“The concern for Republicans is that, amid a divided GOP field, Republican voters will only choose one of their candidates on their ranked-choice ballots rather than ranking multiple options, allowing Kreiss-Tomkins to consolidate a majority,” Cook editor Jessica Taylor wrote in her analysis.

In Nebraska, Cook moved the governor’s race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican,” as polling shows an unusually close race between Gov. Jim Pillen (R) and former state Sen. Lynne Walz (D). Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) shows the incumbent leading Walz by 5.3 points .

In Vermont, Gov. Phil Scott’s (R) race against Democrat Amanda Janoo shifted from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican,” as recent polls have shown a closer than expected contest. The state holds gubernatorial elections every two years, and Scott won reelection in 2024 by more than 50 points.

A recent State Navigate poll of the race found Scott leading by just three points. Taylor writes in her analysis that while Cook is skeptical the race is competitive, the polls showing Scott with declining support are “worth paying attention to.”

In Oklahoma’s open gubernatorial contest, Cook changed its rating from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican.” GOP candidate Mike Mazzei, Oklahoma’s former budget secretary, won a primary runoff in August — likely boosted by President Trump’s endorsement. Mazzei is facing off against state House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson (D).

In Taylor’s write-up, she notes that the Republican Governor’s Association recently purchased more than $2 million in ads to support Mazzei and says that private Democratic polling previously showed a competitive race.

articles.title: Democrats lead Republicans on favorability, economy: Gallup
articles.summary: A new poll found that Democrats lead Republicans on favorability and on the economy as candidates make their final pitches in the weeks leading up to the November midterm elections. The new Gallup poll released Tuesday showed 43 percent of respondents favoring the Democratic Party more than the GOP, which saw support from 35 percent.…
articles.body:
A new poll found that Democrats lead Republicans on favorability and on the economy as candidates make their final pitches in the weeks leading up to the November midterm elections.

The new Gallup poll released Tuesday showed 43 percent of respondents favoring the Democratic Party more than the GOP, which saw support from 35 percent. This marked a 6-point increase for Democrats and a 5-point drop for Republicans since last year .

Gallup has noted that the Democratic Party has typically been viewed more favorably since 1992, averaging 49 percent compared with the Republican Party’s 44 percent average. Both parties hit a majority at least once since 2010, with Democrats seeing 51 percent favorability in 2012 and 51 percent favorability for Republicans in 2020.

Polling showed that Democrats were last viewed more favorably by respondents in September 2021, also at 43 percent, compared to that same poll’s 40 percent for Republicans.

The Democratic Party also won marks on handling the economy, with 50 percent of independents saying Democrats would better handle the economy, and 32 percent say they prefer GOP to handle the economy.

Independents overall view Democrats favorably over Republicans, 40-27, adding that Democrats are better able to handle the country’s most important problems at 39 percent, while 26 percent of respondents said the same of Republicans.

Partisan support for either party on handling the country’s most important problems remains high, with 86 percent of Republicans and 90 percent of Democrats saying their party is better on the issue.

Just over half of respondents prefer Democrats to be able to keep the country prosperous, compared to 37 percent who say the GOP is better capable of keeping the U.S. prosperous.

“The Democratic Party has improved its standing relative to the Republican Party on several measures of public opinion, reversing advantages the GOP held on key issues during much of the Biden administration,” pollsters said. “The shift extends beyond overall party favorability to perceptions of which party is better able to address the nation’s problems, maintain prosperity and protect the country from foreign threats.”

Gallup added that “neither party enjoys a broadly positive public image. Despite the Democratic Party’s current advantages, a majority of Americans view it unfavorably.”

Democrats have seen growing favorability in recent months, with consistent polling showing the party having an advantage going into the midterms. Republicans have campaigned on the successes of the Trump administration, though a rising tide of candidates and incumbents have called for an end to the Iran war to lower energy prices, both of which being a growing concern among voters.

An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll, conducted by AI research platform TrueDot.ai, released Tuesday showed Democrats leading Republicans with 49 percent support to the GOP’s 42 percent on the generic congressional ballot.

The Gallup survey was conducted Sept. 1-17 and included 1,000 respondents. The margin of error is 4 percentage points.
