articles.body:
President Trump will hit the campaign trail in Kansas next week, the Republican National Committee (RNC) announced on Tuesday, as the state’s Senate race grows more competitive.

Trump’s upcoming rally Monday in Wichita is the latest sign Republicans are paying more attention to their chances in Sen. Roger Marshall’s (R-Kan.) reelection bid .

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as a “toss-up,” but gives Marshall an 8-point advantage. A New York Times/Siena College poll released earlier this month showed Marshall and his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton tied in the state.

But Republicans do not appear to be taking any chances on Kansas. The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Republican Senate leadership, is investing $14 million in the race to support Marshall.

The RNC also announced that Trump will travel Tuesday to Greenville, N.C., Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley continues to fall behind his opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper (D).

Trump told reporters last week that he was worried about Whatley’s chances in the state.

“I hope he wins. He was a great leader for the whole Republican Party when I won, and he’d be a great senator,” the president said.

articles.title: Judge rebukes DHS for ‘outrageous’ false statements targeting former FEMA official
articles.summary: A federal judge rebuked the leadership of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for “outrageous” conduct in targeting the former chief financial officer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) after accusing her of wrongly dispersing a grant related to migrant housing. DHS fired Mary Comans over an $80 million grant to New York City…
articles.body:
A federal judge rebuked the leadership of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for “outrageous” conduct in targeting the former chief financial officer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) after accusing her of wrongly dispersing a grant related to migrant housing.

DHS fired Mary Comans over an $80 million grant to New York City allowing for emergency sheltering of migrants, one of many doled out to cities as part of the Shelter and Services Program created by Congress to help pay for the cost of housing migrants.

But shortly after awarding the grant, DHS clawed the money back and accused Comans and others of “unilaterally mak[ing] egregious payments for luxury NYC hotels for migrants,” arguing the move ran afoul of an executive order from President Trump pausing funding to non-profits aiding migrants.

Virginia-based federal magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick noted that such “name-clearing” hearings are rare, but said the move was essential “given the outrageous government conduct, including by those at the highest levels of DHS.”

“For reasons unfathomable to this Court, officials chose to turn the power of the federal government against a singular employee with an impeccable record of public service. In short, Ms. Comans was professionally targeted and personally attacked by government officials for no legitimate reason,” Fitzpatrick wrote.

“The attacks against Ms. Comans were based entirely on false information, and many government officials knew the accusations were untrue at the time they were made. With no regard for the truth and with no consideration for the personal and professional effect on Ms. Comans, government officials exploited their access to mass media outlets to broadcast false information.”

The city of New York sued over the rescission of the grant funding in February of last year, while Comans sued over her termination the next month.

Comans and the awarding of the grant were discussed in public statements from both then Homeland Security Kristi Noem as well as Elon Musk, with Fitzpatrick concluding each “engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans.”

“Armed only with false statements, high-ranking government officials undertook a premeditated campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans, a nonpartisan, career public servant. Their intent was to disseminate false and derogatory information about Ms. Comans as widely as possible,” he wrote.

Fitzpatrick then parsed a laundry list of false statements made in regards to Comans.

“To be clear, it was the stated position of the United States Government that Ms. Comans acted in a criminal manner with a criminal intent. That is untrue. Ms. Comans was publicly accused of knowingly and ‘egregiously’ misspending federal funds. That is untrue. She was accused of laundering ‘forbidden funding.’ That is untrue. She was accused of willfully violating a Presidential Executive Order, the orders of the DHS Secretary, circumventing leadership, and frustrating the will of the American people. That is untrue. She was accused of undermining public safety. That is untrue,” he wrote.

Attorneys for Comans celebrated the ruling.

“Mary Comans served in the federal government for 21 years. Career public servants are people, not pawns, and no one who has devoted their life to serving the American public should have their good name destroyed for partisan, political gain. We are grateful that the court issued this detailed and unprecedented decision to formally correct the record and vindicate Ms. Comans,” attorney Craig Becker of Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement.

DHS did not immediately respond to request for comment.

New York also ultimately regained the funding from the disrupted grant after litigation brought by other cities.

“This is a victory for all federal employees. No federal employee should be defamed to advance false conspiracies of the Trump administration,” said Michael Coen, who was FEMA’s chief of staff during the Obama and Biden administrations.

Zach Schonfeld and Rachel Frazin contributed.

articles.title: Axelrod questions timing of Omar raid weeks before election
articles.summary: Democratic strategist David Axelrod on Monday questioned the timing of the federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home. “We do not know the nature of the probe against Omar. But it is highly unlikely that it’s so serious and urgent that the government felt they needed to act publicly three weeks before the election…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist David Axelrod on Monday questioned the timing of the federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home.

“We do not know the nature of the probe against Omar. But it is highly unlikely that it’s so serious and urgent that the government felt they needed to act publicly three weeks before the election instead of after,” Axelrod said in a post on the social platform X .

“Unless that’s precisely WHY they acted now, not to defeat her–they can’t–but to stir up the muck in MN to try and win a senate seat,” he added.

On Monday morning , federal agents searched Omar’s home in an ongoing criminal investigation. Homeland Security Investigations agents carried out the search, a spokesperson with the Department of Justice (DOJ) told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” the DOJ said in the statement.

Omar blasted the raid on social media, referring to it as “political intimidation.”

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on the social platform X. “For ten years, [President] Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

Trump referred to the Minnesota Democrat as “totally crooked” in his first comments since the raid on Monday.

“Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” Trump told reporters. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”

“I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ [Department of Justice],” he continued. “I have nothing to do with it.”

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ for comment.

articles.title: House Democrats: Guilfoyle’s resignation ‘does not shield her from accountability’
articles.summary: Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee called for further accountability after the White House announced Tuesday that the Trump administration has asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign following reports about her alleged misconduct. “Resigning does not shield her from accountability,” the committee’s Democrats wrote on the social platform X. “Guilfoyle used…
articles.body:
Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee called for further accountability after the White House announced Tuesday that the Trump administration has asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign following reports about her alleged misconduct.

“Resigning does not shield her from accountability,” the committee’s Democrats wrote on the social platform X . “Guilfoyle used her position as a Trump official to get rich, while American families struggle with the cost of living.”

The statement continued: “Congress must conduct oversight to understand how this happened and hold the admin accountable.”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, also committed to continuing to investigate Guilfoyle.

“While your time as Ambassador to Greece may be coming to an end, our investigation has not,” he wrote on X . “We have asked you a series of questions, and we look forward to your responses.”

The Wall Street Journal first reported last week that MAGA donor Eric Deters accused Guilfoyle of asking him to wire her $100,000 to pay off her American Express bill ahead of her 2025 confirmation hearing and instructed him to do so without leaving a paper trail.

The Journal later released a separate report over the weekend with new allegations that Guilfoyle bragged about her connections to wealthy Greek businessmen who bankrolled her luxury travel.

Guilfoyle denied the allegations in a statement addressing her resignation, saying she would “vigorously” defend herself.

“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,” she wrote.

The accusations triggered a slew of investigations into her conduct, including probes from the State Department and in Congress.

Following the news of her ouster, Trump on Tuesday downplayed her closeness to his family. Guilfoyle was engaged to the president’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr. until the two split in 2024. They were first linked together in 2018.

“She wasn’t a member of my family. I guess she dated my son a long time ago,” Trump said.

He added that he “didn’t like” what he read in the recent swirl of negative stories detailing embarrassing and possibly illegal conduct ahead of her confirmation and while serving in her diplomatic position.

articles.title: Zacharia’s first spin at White House podium draws rocky reviews
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was met with a barrage of criticism following her first briefing in her new role, leading some to question the future of her tenure shortly after she was tapped for the job. Zacharia on Tuesday delivered a roughly 14-minute briefing and took questions from only three outlets. She notably…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was met with a barrage of criticism following her first briefing in her new role, leading some to question the future of her tenure shortly after she was tapped for the job.

Zacharia on Tuesday delivered a roughly 14-minute briefing and took questions from only three outlets. She notably broke news when she told a reporter the administration asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her role as U.S. ambassador to Greece, but she wrapped the briefing shortly thereafter.

One former White House official characterized Zacharia’s performance as “fine,” noting “it was clear that this was just a warmup.”

“Breitbart and Fox? OK. She did fine, but this was hardly a true test,” the official said.

“Nice job on breaking the news about Guilfoyle though,” they added.

Critics were quick to note Zacharia looked visibly nervous during the briefing and said it looked like she ended it prematurely.

“The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci,” former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci wrote on the social platform X . Scaramucci infamously served in the role during the first Trump administration for 11 days before he was fired.

Zacharia replaced former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who announced she was leaving the administration earlier this year.

Leavitt was seen as the gold standard for Trump-era press secretaries, ready at any moment to go on attack mode against the news media while strategically forging relationships with the press behind the scenes.

Before her role in Trump’s second administration, Leavitt served under former first-term press secretary Kayleigh McEnany, who was also praised for her unwavering defense of Trump and her combative style.

“Love them or hate them: Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt came out swinging in their first press briefings. They were sharp, confident, prepared, and proved they had the chops for the job right out of the gate,” said Sarah Matthews, former deputy White House press secretary during the first Trump administration, in a post on X.

“Katie Zacharia? A rather underwhelming debut. Three questions, including one from the new media seat, and a heavy reliance on her notes. Not exactly in command of the briefing room,” continued Matthews, who has since become an outspoken Trump critic.

Others argued Zacharia should be given more slack, noting Tuesday was her second day on the job.

“We were told she was getting the job on Friday, and she rolls out here on what, what’s today, Tuesday?” said one Republican strategist.

The strategist argued that it took past secretaries like McEnany and Leavitt weeks and months to truly get the hang of the role of White House press secretary, but then noted their experience working for Trump on the campaign benefited them.

“They were taking live fire from the campaign for months before they were doing this job,” the strategist said, referring to McEnany and Leavitt, as well as former press secretaries Sean Spicer and Sarah Huckabee Sanders.

Zacharia “was going on TV interviews, but she wasn’t taking that live fire, breaking news as it happens,” the strategist noted. “When you’re on the campaign trail or even during the transition because you’re taking live fire every day, once you get behind [the podium], it’s no different being in the Brady Room than it is on the campaign trail or on Air Force One.”

Zacharia started out the briefing conventionally, touting the president’s agenda for just more than eight minutes before taking the questions.

She took her first question from the conservative outlet Breitbart in the new media seat, a usually safe option Leavitt and her substitutes took in the past, before taking questions from Fox News and the Daily Mail.

When asked by Fox News’s Peter Doocy if the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Zacharia said she would get back to him on that. But the newsiest bit of the briefing came when Zacharia told the Daily Mail the administration asked Guilfoyle to step down from her post after a week of negative headlines.

The former White House official noted Zacharia would really be tested when she takes questions from more adversarial news outlets.

“Maybe we start with asking a question from somebody other than the official media outlet of Team Trump, and then work our way up from there,” the former official said.

“I’m sure this was by design. Ease her into the job, which makes the complete sense,” they added.

Zacharia’s first briefing room performance is not the only thing coming under scrutiny. The newsletter Popular Information has raised questions about Zacharia’s legal career after she has been described as an attorney in a number of media appearances.

The new press secretary was asked Tuesday about which state she passed the bar in, to which she responded, “when I moved to China.”

When asked to clarify where Zacharia passed the bar exam, a White House official said she moved to China with her husband after graduating due to his job at a U.S. private equity firm, and she worked on international transaction law.

The White House has so far offered glowing reviews of Zacharia’s performance, describing it as a “powerful, inaugural briefing” in an email blast to reporters on Tuesday.

“Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement. “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.”

Zacharia will get more time in the spotlight this week as she hits the campaign trail with Trump, starting with Alaska on Tuesday.

However, those close to Trump note it’s his opinion that is ultimately the only one that matters.

“I thought she was very good,” Trump told reporters outside the White House, standing alongside Zacharia, when he was asked about the briefing.

President Trump is making an unusual campaign stop in Alaska Tuesday, where a once-reliably-Republican Senate seat is now firmly in play just three weeks before the midterms.

The visit comes just over a week after Vice President Vance campaigned for Sullivan in Fairbanks, underscoring the attention the race is getting from the White House.

Trump’s trip also comes amid frustration over high energy costs and his controversial diesel deal with Russia, which has drawn criticism from the other Alaska senator, Lisa Murkowski (R). His most recent visit to the Last Frontier State was in August 2025 during a summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The event in Wasilla, Alaska, is scheduled to begin at 7:30 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: House Democrat introduces bill seeking to cut ICE, CBP, replace DHS
articles.summary: Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) introduced a bill Tuesday to overhaul U.S. immigration agencies, including replacing the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) with a new “community-centered” department. The “Reimagining Safety Act” would abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), as well as dismantle DHS, replacing it with a new agency called…
articles.body:
Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) introduced a bill Tuesday to overhaul U.S. immigration agencies, including replacing the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) with a new “community-centered” department.

The “Reimagining Safety Act” would abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), as well as dismantle DHS, replacing it with a new agency called the “Department of Community Safety.” The bill would preserve non-immigration functions of DHS, including the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Transportation Security Administration.

“Every person dead in detention, shot or killed by ICE and CBP, every neighbor deported to a third country, every family separated … is a reason DHS must be dismantled and something new must take its place,” Ramirez said in a statement.

Ramirez, a member of the House Homeland Security Committee and a frequent ICE critic, has repeatedly called to abolish ICE and dismantle DHS in the past. After federal agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens as part of an immigration operation in Minneapolis in January, Ramirez marched alongside protesters in the city.

President Trump’s immigration agenda has become unpopular with voters, despite it being one of his strongest issues in the 2024 campaign. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 1 found that just 39 percent of Americans approve of the president’s handling of immigration.

Trump allies have suggested Trump’s efforts to end illegal immigration to the country were successful, and that voters are not giving him credit for those wins. His critics argue his strict policies going after legal and illegal immigrants in the U.S. have turned off voters.

Some Democrats have avoided calls to abolish ICE entirely, though the idea did gain traction following those fatal shootings. A January Economist/YouGov poll found that more Americans supported abolishing ICE than opposed it, 46 percent to 43 percent.
